excerpt: An AI Agent-Ready 2D Modeling and Animation Tool. Contribute to getzipzi/zipzi-2d development by creating an account on GitHub.
content_html:
English · 简体中文 · 日本語

An open-source 2D modeling and animation tool for creating alongside AI.

You shape the artwork. Your AI agent helps with the modeling work. Zipzi connects a visual desktop editor with a Python API, so you and your agent can inspect and edit the same model, share undo history, and build on each other’s changes.

Zipzi 2D is an open-source alternative to Live2D Cubism Editor, built with Rust and GPUI. Its name comes from Cantonese 摺紙 (zip3 zi2), meaning “origami”.

Download Alpha · Python SDK · Report an issue · Contribute

Early development: There is no stable release yet. APIs and file formats may change. The editor supports macOS and Windows.

  • Open source and commercial friendly — Create, refine, and use your models commercially with an open-source editor and an MIT-licensed SDK.
  • Native and high performance — Built with Rust and GPUI for low memory usage and responsive editing, even with complex models and dense meshes.
  • Agent-ready — Create from scratch, collaborate with AI, or import an existing model for further refinement.
zipzi-2d-demo.mp4

Your editor. Your AI agent. One model.

Describe what you want to your AI coding agent. It uses the Python SDK to inspect models, view rendered images and make edits you can review and undo in the editor. You and your agent work on the same document, with shared undo history.

Bring your own Python-capable agent and point it to the SDK guide.

First code: let AI give every mesh a meaningful name

You describe the task; your AI agent writes and runs the code. The examples below were generated by an AI coding agent and tested against a running Editor. They show how the agent works through the Python SDK—you do not need to write these scripts yourself. Your role is to explain what you want and review the results in the editor.

Ask your agent: “Look at every mesh and give it a meaningful name.”

Install the Python client (CPython 3.14), start a compatible Editor with GPU observation support, and open one model. An image-capable coding agent can run the following two steps.

1. The agent observes every mesh. Its generated script exports one image per mesh, with its wireframe highlighted over the textured model, plus a JSON naming worksheet. observe supplies visual evidence; the agent supplies the semantic interpretation.

import json
from pathlib import Path
from uuid import uuid4

import zipzi
from zipzi import inspection, observation, spatial

output = Path("mesh-review-" + uuid4().hex[:8]).resolve()
output.mkdir()

with zipzi.connect() as runtime:
    sessions = runtime.sessions.list()
    if len(sessions) != 1:
        raise RuntimeError("Open exactly one model for this example.")
    session = runtime.sessions.attach(sessions[0].id)

    # Follow every page: a single list() call may not contain all meshes.
    meshes, cursor, source = [], None, None
    while True:
        page = session.meshes.list(cursor=cursor)
        if source is None:
            source = page.source
        if page.source != source:
            raise RuntimeError("Model changed; restart the inspection.")
        meshes.extend(page.items)
        cursor = page.next_cursor
        if cursor is None:
            break

    rows = []
    for index, mesh in enumerate(meshes):
        # Use this mesh's bounds to frame it, including hidden geometry.
        # {} evaluates default parameter values, not the editor's current pose.
        query = spatial.Bounds(
            targets=(spatial.MeshTarget(value=mesh.id),), include_hidden=True,
        )
        bounds = session.modeling.spatial(
            ({},), (query,), expected=source,
        ).wait().value.frames[0].results[0].value.model_bounds
        row = dict(id=mesh.id, old_name=mesh.name, new_name=mesh.name, image=None)
        if bounds is not None:
            x0, y0, x1, y1 = bounds
            margin = max(x1 - x0, y1 - y0, 1.0) * 0.15
            view = observation.View(
                width=768, height=768,
                roi=(x0 - margin, y0 - margin, x1 + margin, y1 + margin),
                topology=observation.Overlay(
                    targets=(observation.MeshTarget(value=mesh.id),),
                    wireframe=True, include_hidden=True,
                ),
            )
            # Freeze all observations to the inventory's source. If the model
            # changes, the SDK refuses stale reads; rerun instead of mixing them.
            images = session.modeling.observe(({},), view, expected=source).wait()
            report = inspection.save(images, output / f"mesh-{index:04d}")
            row["image"] = str(report.images[0])
        rows.append(row)

    # SessionId is a typed handle: store its fields for the second script.
    worksheet = output / "names.json"
    worksheet.write_text(json.dumps(
        dict(session_id=dict(runtime=session.id.runtime, serial=session.id.serial),
             meshes=rows), indent=2, ensure_ascii=False,
    ), encoding="utf-8")
    print(worksheet)

Have the agent open each exported PNG, identify the highlighted mesh in context, and edit only new_name in names.json. Keep IDs and old_name intact. The overlay selects diagnostic geometry, not isolated artwork: surrounding textures remain visible, and hidden or occluded artwork may still be ambiguous. Keep the original name for uncertain or image-less entries, or inspect additional poses before naming them.

2. The agent applies the semantic names together. After you review the proposed names, the agent writes and runs the following script with the path to names.json. You do not need to copy the code or run a terminal command. Keep the same model open and unchanged between inspection and application.

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import zipzi

review = json.loads(Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
rows = review["meshes"]
if len({row["id"] for row in rows}) != len(rows):
    raise ValueError("Duplicate mesh IDs in the worksheet.")
if any(not isinstance(row["new_name"], str) or not row["new_name"].strip()
       for row in rows):
    raise ValueError("Every mesh needs a nonempty name.")

with zipzi.connect() as runtime:
    # Rebuild the typed handle; a restarted Editor requires a new inspection.
    session = runtime.sessions.attach(zipzi.SessionId(**review["session_id"]))
    # All renames commit together as one undo step. A missing mesh or changed
    # original name aborts the edit instead of leaving a partly renamed model.
    with session.edit("AI: semantic mesh names") as edit:
        for row in rows:
            current = edit.meshes.get(row["id"]).value
            if current.name != row["old_name"]:
                raise RuntimeError("Mesh changed; inspect the model again.")
            if row["new_name"] != row["old_name"]:
                edit.meshes.rename(
                    row["id"], row["new_name"], expected_name=row["old_name"],
                )
    print("Review the names in the editor. Undo to revert, or save to keep them.")

No project save happens automatically. The name check detects renamed or removed meshes, not every possible geometry or texture change; repeat the inspection if the model has changed. For more workflows, see the capability guide.

Built for hands-on creation, too

Work with meshes, parameters, deformers and BlendShapes, then bring them together in the animation workspace. Generate mesh geometry or refine it by hand. Mesh Edit lets you work on the posed model or switch to the source image, while resampling stored shapes as the geometry changes.

Python scripts can also run independently with a local Runtime for automation outside the editor. Explore the Python SDK for modeling, animation authoring, previews and inspection.

Try Zipzi 2D

  • Use the editor: Download an Alpha build from GitHub Releases. Check the release notes for the available platform builds and requirements.
  • Automate with Python: Follow the installation and connection guide. The SDK currently requires CPython 3.14.
  • Build your own tools: Explore the Rust SDK for programmatic authoring.

Current capabilities

Area What you can work with
Modeling Meshes, parameters, keyforms, parts, deformers, BlendShapes and Glue
Animation Motion, expression, physics and pose authoring; animation previews
Project I/O PSD import and Cubism-related formats, including Model3/MOC3, projects and runtime sidecars; support and loss rules vary by format and direction
Automation Python sessions, batch edits, shared undo/redo, project operations and model inspection
Platforms macOS and Windows

See the SDK capability guide for details. GPU inspection requires a compatible host and usable GPU. Format support does not imply lossless round trips for every model.

Contributing

Try an Alpha build and tell us what gets in your way. For bug reports, include the build version, platform and steps to reproduce; share model assets only when you have permission to do so.

For code contributions, start with the repository map, editor guide or Python SDK guide. The documentation index covers deeper references. Development commands and focused test selection are below.

Development

Use Rust 1.95 or newer, uv 0.10.7 or newer, and CPython 3.14. The macOS Editor requires Xcode Command Line Tools and a Metal-capable GPU. The Windows Editor requires MSVC, the Windows SDK and a usable GPU. Run these commands from the repository root:

uv sync --locked
python3 tools/workspace/cargo_domain.py --check

# Focused SDK development
cargo test --locked -p zipzi-sdk --test integration physics_editing::

# Native Editor (macOS)
cargo run --locked -p zipzi-editor
./tools/test-editor.sh fast timeline::

# Repository tooling tests; no native application build
uv run --locked python tools/test_tools.py

For the Python SDK, ./tools/test-sdk.sh python refreshes its native adapter and runs Local/Connected behavior and static types. python-connected installs the pure wheel and validates real subprocess host discovery and session binding; add --editor-host /absolute/path/to/zipzi-editor for the current desktop host. Root pyproject.toml and uv.lock manage development tools.

Tests

Focused test commands and coverage

Choose the smallest gate covering the change, then broaden when needed. Run commands from the repository root; inspect available modes with ./tools/test-sdk.sh --help, ./tools/test-editor.sh --help or uv run --locked python tools/test_tools.py --help.

Changed area Starting command
One Rust crate/module cargo test --locked -p <crate> --lib <filter>; add its integration target when relevant
Runtime ownership/jobs/events ./tools/test-sdk.sh runtime
Local protocol / installed Python client ./tools/test-sdk.sh python-connected
SDK authoring behavior ./tools/test-sdk.sh fast <filter>
Editor adaptive mesh generation ./tools/test-editor.sh fast adaptive_mesh::; ./tools/test-editor.sh fast mesh_generation::
SDK alpha mesh generation ./tools/test-sdk.sh mesh
wgpu backend / local GPU parity cargo test --locked -p zipzi-render-wgpu --tests; host selection
Editor coordination ./tools/test-editor.sh fast <filter>
Editor UI (macOS/Metal) ./tools/test-editor.sh ui <filter>
Runtime Python SDK (zipzi-python), Local/Connected and types ./tools/test-sdk.sh python (scope)
Shared authoring contract / isolated Python generation cargo test --locked -p zipzi-contract; uv run --locked python tools/test_tools.py -p test_python_codegen.py
Runtime GPU observation / inspection (usable GPU required) ./tools/test-sdk.sh python --observation
Python complete-call recovery, Edit state and Job timeout ./tools/test-sdk.sh python --recovery (optional P3ARecovery.test_name)
Python collection pages, Session detach/close and offline catalog ./tools/test-sdk.sh python --discovery
Installed new client, host discovery and session binding ./tools/test-sdk.sh python-connected (optional --editor-host /absolute/path/to/zipzi-editor)
Repository tools uv run --locked python tools/test_tools.py -p test_<tool>.py

Filters and filenames are placeholders; omit them to run the selected gate. For a crate's integration targets, inspect its README and tests/, or list cases with cargo test --locked -p <crate> --test <target> -- --list. Editor shell gates clear ZIPZI_DEV_SESSION_DIR; clear it explicitly when running Editor Cargo tests directly.

Full coverage, prerequisites and CI define regression, stress, native acceptance and packaged-wheel gates. Both domain scripts default to expensive full runs when no mode is supplied. Plain cargo test selects only zipzi-core, zipzi-project and zipzi-sdk. Tooling tests belong in tools/tests/, crate tests stay with their crate, and shared data belongs in fixtures/.

All owned crates share the root Cargo workspace and lockfile. Local models belong in models/local/; see the model inventory. Source archives, Python wheels and macOS app bundles have separate distribution checks.

License and third-party rights

SDK components use MIT; Editor components use GPL-3.0-only. LICENSING identifies scopes and shared-file origins; third-party notices retain dependency and benchmark exceptions.
